title: Question 3
stem:
A car of mass $1500\text{ kg}$ is travelling along a straight horizontal road at constant velocity $v$. The car is subject to a total resistive force $F$, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Show that the power $P$ developed by the engine in overcoming the total resistive force is given by the equation

$$P = Fv.$$

markscheme_points.text: P = Fd / t = Fv or P = Fvt / t = Fv

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what power means in words - how quickly work is done - and what work means when a force pushes a car forward.
Hint 2: Think about the distance travelled in a short time $t$ at constant speed $v$, then put that distance into the work expression and divide by $t$.
parts.proper_answer: Work done against $F$ in distance $d$ is $W = Fd$. Power $P = W/t = Fd/t = Fv$ since $d/t = v$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what work and power mean**
Imagine the engine pushing the car forward just hard enough to balance the resistive force $F$. In a distance $d$ the work it does is force times distance in the direction of motion. So $$W = Fd$$ This is the useful energy transferred in overcoming resistance.

Step 2: **Turn rate of working into $Fv$**
Power is how fast that work is done: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ Put the work expression in: $$P = \frac{Fd}{t} = F\left(\frac{d}{t}\right)$$ For constant speed, distance per unit time is the speed, $d/t = v$. So $$P = Fv$$

enrichment.label: (a)
key_concepts: work done by a constant force
power as rate of doing work
relation between distance, speed and time

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: Show that the increase in gravitational potential energy of the car in a time of $1.0\text{ s}$ is $46000\text{ J}$.

markscheme_points.text: increase of gravitational potential energy of car in 1.0 s = 1500 × 9.81 × 30 × sin6.0 = 46 000 J

hints: Hint 1: Focus on vertical height gained, not distance along the slope. Sketch the right-angled triangle with the 6.0 degree slope and see how height relates to the 30 m travelled in 1.0 s.
Hint 2: Use $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ with $m = 1500\text{ kg}$ and your value for $\Delta h$, and check the result rounds to about $4.6 \times 10^4\text{ J}$.
parts.proper_answer: Distance along slope in 1.0 s $= 30 \times 1.0 = 30\text{ m}$. Vertical gain $h = 30\sin 6.0^{\circ} = 3.14\text{ m}$. $\Delta E_p = mgh = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 30\sin 6.0^{\circ} \approx 4.6 \times 10^4\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find how far up the slope and how high**
In $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ at $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ the car travels along the slope: $$d = vt = 30 \times 1.0 = 30\text{ m}$$ Only the vertical part of this counts for gravitational potential energy. From the triangle: $$h = d \sin 6.0^{\circ} = 30 \sin 6.0^{\circ}$$ That gives $h \approx 3.14\text{ m}$. A common slip is to use $d$ directly as $h$.

Step 2: **Calculate the gain in potential energy**
Gravitational potential energy gain is: $$\Delta E_p = mgh$$ Put in the numbers: $$\Delta E_p = 1500 \times 9.81 \times 30 \times \sin 6.0^{\circ}$$ $$\Delta E_p \approx 4.6 \times 10^4\text{ J}$$ This matches the required $46000\text{ J}$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use the information in (b)(i) to determine the power developed by the engine to move the car up the slope.

markscheme_points.text: (Power to overcome total resistive forces) = 1600 × 30 = 48 000 W

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two jobs the engine does every second on the slope - pushing against the 1600 N resistive force and lifting the car to give it extra gravitational potential energy.
Hint 2: Combine the rate of working against resistance from part (a) with the energy per second from (b)(i) to get total power in watts.
parts.proper_answer: Power against resistance $= Fv = 1600 \times 30 = 48000\text{ W}$. Power for GPE gain $= 46000/1.0 = 46000\text{ W}$. Total $P = 48000 + 46000 = 9.4 \times 10^4\text{ W}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Split the power into two parts**
At constant speed kinetic energy does not change, so all engine power goes to two stores: work against resistive forces plus gain of gravitational potential energy. Using $P = Fv$ from (a): $$P_{resistive} = Fv = 1600 \times 30 = 48000\text{ W}$$

Step 2: **Add the lifting power**
From (b)(i), $46000\text{ J}$ of potential energy is gained every $1.0\text{ s}$, so: $$P_{lift} = \frac{\Delta E_p}{t} = \frac{46000}{1.0} = 46000\text{ W}$$ Total engine power: $$P = 48000 + 46000 = 94000\text{ W} = 9.4 \times 10^4\text{ W}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: The car picks up a passenger and then continues up the slope at the same speed as in (b). State and explain the effect, if any, that the passenger has on:

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: the air resistance acting on the car

markscheme_points.text: Air resistance is the same, as the speed is the same

hints: Hint 1: Think about what controls air resistance - speed, shape and size - and decide which of these changes when a passenger sits inside the car.
parts.proper_answer: No change. Air resistance depends on speed and shape, both unchanged, so air resistance is the same.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why air resistance stays the same**
Air resistance (drag) depends mainly on speed through the air and on the shape and frontal area of the car. A passenger inside does not change the outside shape and the speed is kept at $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$. So the air flow past the car is identical and the air resistance is unchanged.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the power developed by the engine.

markscheme_points.text: Mass / weight has increased so (power will) increase

hints: Hint 1: Think about how total mass links to weight and to the extra $mgh$ needed each second when climbing at the same vertical rate.
parts.proper_answer: Power increases because total mass (and weight) is larger, so more gravitational potential energy must be supplied per second at the same speed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why more power is needed with extra mass**
Adding a passenger increases total mass $m$ and hence weight $mg$. The rate of gain of potential energy $mg \times$ vertical speed increases, and the component of weight down the slope also increases. To keep the same constant speed up the slope the engine must do more work per second, so the power developed increases.
